title: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns
hook: brown, white, red, dappled, dark: one hymn looks at the plants before it asks them for anything

segments.voice: Yesterday, from the Atharva Veda's healing hymns, a cough sent flying: as the mind flies, as an arrow, as the sun's rays over the sea. What did you send off on a long breath? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.
screen: `GIVE IT A DIRECTION, NOT A FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Brown, white, red, dappled, dark. That's not a paint chart. It's how one Atharva Veda hymn begins its roll call of the plants. Before it asks them for anything, it looks at them, and sorts them by color, the way a kid sorts crayons or a cook lines up vegetables on a cutting board. An empty lot in summer holds the same crowd: weeds and wildflowers and grasses, all different, many of them without a name to a passerby. The hymn calls them up one color at a time, and then calls them all. Today: the plants, called by name.
screen: `BROWN, WHITE, RED, DAPPLED, DARK.` → `NOT A PAINT CHART.` → `A ROLL CALL OF PLANTS.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda has a long hymn to the plants. It opens, in paraphrase: the brown ones, the white ones, the red ones, the dappled, the dark and the black, all the plants, we call on. It goes on to ask them to protect the one who is sick. The Sanskrit word for these plants is oshadhi, a plant or herb, especially one that heals. The Rig Veda has a hymn to the plants too. It speaks to them with a startling word. Plants, it says in paraphrase, mothers, I speak to you as goddesses. Mothers. Not ingredients. Not supplies. And the same Rig Veda hymn says who a healer is. The one in whom the plants gather, the way kings gather in an assembly, that wise one is called a healer. So the healer isn't someone with a title. The healer is someone the plants seem to crowd around: someone who knows them, by color, by name, by where they grow. Knowing comes before asking. One honest note. The hymns don't come with pictures, and which plant each old name meant isn't always clear today. And these are hymns, not prescriptions. Nothing here tells anyone what to take for an illness. What they do offer is a way of looking. The basil on the windowsill, the onion on the counter, the weed in the sidewalk crack: each one has a color, a shape, a name. The hymn treats noticing them as the first step.
screen: `BROWN, WHITE, RED, DAPPLED, DARK.` · `OSHADHI: A PLANT THAT HEALS.` · `MOTHERS, SPOKEN TO AS GODDESSES.` · `A HEALER IS WHERE PLANTS GATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call one plant by name. Find something green or grown within reach: a houseplant, an apple, tea leaves, the wood of a table, the cotton of your shirt. Look at it closely. Name its color as plainly as the hymn does. Brown. Red. Dappled. Then think of what it took to get here: soil, rain, sun, someone's hands. Stay with it, just looking. If you pray, you can hold it there in thanks. The bell holds the time.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, a hymn that calls the plants by color, and a neighbor hymn that calls them mothers. Today's word.
screen: `THE ATHARVA VEDA'S HEALING HYMNS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, learn the name of one plant you pass every day and never noticed. Say it once when you pass it. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu households and temples give honor to plants such as tulsi, and the Vedic hymns to the plants are kept in recitation; Ayurvedic tradition later developed its own learning about plants used in healing.
